uncited: Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations address the high memory consumption and overfitting issues inherent in dense voxel-based radiance fields by modeling the scene as a factorized 4D tensor [S1].

Unlike [Direct Voxel Grid Optimization](4694-direct-voxel-grid-optimization.md), which stores independent features per voxel, this family exploits the low-rank structure of geometry and appearance to correlate the entire field, reducing space complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n)$ or $O(n^2)$ [S1].

It sets itself apart from [NeRF](4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) by replacing multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with compact vector and matrix factors, enabling significantly faster reconstruction and smaller model sizes [S1].
All methods in this family represent the radiance field as a low-rank tensor decomposition, typically using Canonical Polyadic (CP) or Vector-Matrix (VM) formats [S1].
The core mechanism replaces the implicit function of an MLP or the dense grid of a voxel field with a set of global mode vectors and matrices [S1].

For a 4D radiance field $\mathcal{F}(x, y, z, \theta)$, where $(x,y,z)$ are spatial coordinates and $\theta$ represents view-dependent parameters, the field is approximated by a sum of rank-1 components [S1].
In the Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition, the density $\sigma$ and appearance features $\mathbf{c}$ are computed by interpolating mode vectors and matrices [S1].
For a component $r$, the density contribution is a sum of terms like $\mathbf{v}_X(x) \cdot \mathbf{M}_{YZ}(y,z)$, where $\mathbf{v}$ is a vector and $\mathbf{M}$ is a matrix [S1].
This structure allows for efficient trilinear interpolation and differentiable rendering [S1].
The training process typically employs a coarse-to-fine strategy [S1].

Optimization begins at a low resolution $N_0^3$ (e.g., $128^3$) and upsamples the tensor factors at specific iteration steps (e.g., 2000, 3000, 4000) using linear interpolation for vectors and bilinear interpolation for matrices [S1].

Regularization is critical to prevent overfitting; L1 norm loss on factors encourages sparsity, while Total Variation (TV) loss promotes smoothness, particularly for datasets with few views or imperfect capture [S1].

The concept of tensor decomposition for radiance fields was introduced by [TensoRF](3026-tensorf.md), which demonstrated that radiance fields exhibit low-rank structures in both geometry and appearance [S1].
TensoRF bridges this gap by using tensor factorization to achieve both speed and compactness [S1].

The joint optimization variant addresses the instability of optimizing poses with voxel-based representations by leveraging the spectral bias and smoothness properties of the tensor factors [11498-joint-optimization-of-camera-pose-and-decomposed-low-rank-te.md].
